title: Extended Detection and Response
summary: Extended detection and response, or XDR, is an architectural approach that collects telemetry from several security control points, such as endpoint agents, network sensors, mail gateways, identity providers and cloud workloads, into one place where it is correlated, searched and acted on. The problem it addresses is that endpoint detection and response sees only the host and a security information and event management platform sees only the logs it was given, so an intrusion that starts in email, moves through identity and ends on a laptop appears as three unrelated fragments. XDR binds those fragments into one investigation view and, in most products, offers response actions across the contributing controls rather than only on endpoints. Detections lean on correlation across sources, which reduces the number of isolated alerts but shifts the work to making sure each source's events are normalised and useful. Vendors implement it either as a closed suite of their own agents or as an open platform that ingests third-party feeds, and the two differ sharply in coverage and lock-in. The mistake people usually make is buying an XDR product and expecting correlation to work while telemetry from important systems is missing or arriving with poor field quality.

beginner.definition: Extended detection and response, or XDR, joins security information from many parts of the company. It collects data from laptops, networks, email, cloud systems and login services. Then it looks for one story across all of them. The team can search and act from a single place.
beginner.whyItMatters: Real attacks move between systems. A bad email leads to a stolen password, which leads to a laptop. If each tool sees only its own part, nobody sees the whole picture. XDR connects those parts so an alert makes sense. It also reduces the flood of separate alerts that tires out a security team.
howItWorks: Agents and sensors are installed so each important system reports what happens.
Their events are sent to one platform in a common, comparable format.
The platform links events that share a user, a device or a time window.
Detection rules look for chains of behaviour across several sources at once.
An analyst opens one case that shows the full sequence from start to finish.
Response actions such as isolating a device can be started from that same view.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital where each department keeps its own notes. The x-ray team sees a scan, the pharmacy sees a prescription, and the night desk sees an admission. Nobody spots the pattern until one shared record links them. That shared record also lets a nurse act quickly, because the whole story is in front of them.
takeaways: XDR is about connected data, not about one clever detection rule.
Missing or messy telemetry quietly ruins the correlation you bought it for.
Fewer, richer alerts still need analysts who can investigate and respond.

objectives: Explain what extended detection and response is and which gap it is designed to close.
Compare XDR with endpoint-only detection and with a general log management platform.
Describe how normalisation and cross-source correlation produce a single investigation view.
Identify the telemetry sources that must be onboarded for XDR to be effective.
Recognise implementation risks such as incomplete coverage, poor data quality and vendor lock-in.
